item.title: Strategy dips on bad MSCI World Index news
item.dc:creator: REDACTED
item.description:
A powerful committee adopted “non-operating company” rules that could remove Strategy from the prestigious MSCI World Index.

The post Strategy dips on bad MSCI World Index news appeared first on Protos.
item.content:encoded:
Strategy’s stock price dipped 4% in after-hours trading yesterday as traders speculated about its removal from the MSCI World Index.

The stock indexation giant announced on Thursday that it will adopt rules removing “non-operating companies” from its Global Investable Market Indexes, including its MSCI World Index that benefits from substantial, passive investment inflows. 

Strategy is the biggest name those rules could remove, and the company’s MSTR common stock immediately traded 4% lower within 20 minutes of the closing bell after news of the rule change disseminated.

The timing of the rule change aligns with MSCI’s November 2026 Index Review, effective as of the close on November 30. Strategy isn’t currently a confirmed removal, it’s specifically named as under threat of removal. 

The finalized list of affected constituents will arrive on November 11.

This is the second fright that Strategy shareholders have had to endure about the MSCI World Index and its passive flows in 2026. Indeed, on January 6, MSCI shelved its first opportunity to remove Strategy from its World Index. 

Read more: Strategy’s STRC gives hedge funds a new reason to short MSTR

MSCI has named Strategy as a potential World Index removal in November

MSCI’s new methodology works in two steps. A company whose “operating” assets fall short of half of its “total” assets moves to a five-ratio exclusion screening phase.

Because Strategy holds the vast majority of its assets as non-operating, passive BTC investment, the company would be subjected to this screening phase.

Next, if MSCI flags the company on at least four of five “ratios,” a stock becomes ineligible. 

Removal requires failing the screens in each of the two most recent annual filing periods, which can predate the rules’ adoption. 

An impact list published alongside the adopted rules flags Strategy. Its float-adjusted market value, about $40 billion as of October 9, dwarfs the size of every other stock on the list of potential removals.

Lobbying for MSCI inclusion

Strategy founder Saylor and his CEO Phong Le have actively campaigned against the removal. Their company even has a dedicated subpage on its website dedicated to lobbying for continued MSCI indexation.

In an August 31 letter, for example, Saylor and CEO Phong Le called the proposal “discriminatory, arbitrary, and misguided.” They also warned the rules “would profoundly harm MSCI’s reputation as a reliable and neutral index provider.” 

The letter urges MSCI to “remain what it has held itself out to be for decades: a mirror of the market, not an arbiter of it.”

Saylor kept the same energy on television two days before the decision. On October 13, he told Bloomberg Crypto that MSCI’s position was “disappointing.”

JPMorgan estimated in November 2025, during an earlier threat of de-indexation for Strategy, that MSCI exclusion alone could mean $2.8 billion of outflows for Strategy.

Indeed, Strategy’s August consultation response puts MSCI-linked fund ownership at about 3.1% of its basic shares, roughly 13 million shares.

item.title: Ledger roasted over $849 device launch after $86M hack
item.dc:creator: REDACTED
item.description:
Ledger has been accused of failing to “read the room” after it unveiled its $849 Atom wallet days after suffering an $86M draining hack.

The post Ledger roasted over $849 device launch after $86M hack appeared first on Protos.
item.content:encoded:
Ledger has been accused of failing to “read the room” after the company unveiled its new $849 Atom wallet device just days after falling victim to an $86 million draining hack which led to it suspending multiple resellers.

Users on X have called Ledger’s Atom announcement the “worst timing ever,” with others suggesting that the announcement should have been delayed. 

Read more: Ledger asks more Southeast Asia resellers to halt wallet sales

The Atom, which Ledger says is “not designed to replace your phone,” is a security-focused Android device that looks like a phone but without the ability to make calls and send texts. 

According to The Verge, it will use an eSIM that will be restricted to data capabilities only. Users can still download apps, so in practice, data can still be used for internet-based messages and calls. 

The relatively small size of previous Ledger wallets meant users could at least keep them in a pocket without much trouble. However, it remains to be seen whether they’ll be willing to carry around what is essentially a second phone.

It runs on Android OS and Ledger-OS, its own system that can handle “transactions, logins, and sensitive data.” The device will also come with a so-called “privacy switch” that claims to cut “the camera and mic at the circuit level.”

Ledger says hack was work of ‘organized criminal group’

Last week, Ledger users suffered a more-than-$86 million draining attack that used spyware implanted in devices sold by official Malaysian reseller CryptoBilis.

Ledger revealed today that a “highly organized criminal group” spent “millions” installing spyware onto its wallets.  

It claims the attackers “built their own logistics and technology infrastructure with seeds collector servers, draining and laundering infrastructures.”

Ledger expanded suspension of official reseller wallet sales

Ledger also announced this week that it was asking 23 official resellers across South Asia to suspend sales following the discovery of tampered devices. 

It also revealed yesterday that it couldn’t find “any sign of tampering” with devices from its official German reseller MediaMrkt, and that “no loss of funds related to implants has been reported anywhere in Europe.”

item.title: CoreWeave halved since joining Nasdaq 100 as insiders sold $740 million
item.dc:creator: REDACTED
item.description:
Insiders have dumped hundreds of millions of dollars of CoreWeave stock as shares have dropped more than 46% since it joined the Nasdaq 100.

The post CoreWeave halved since joining Nasdaq 100 as insiders sold $740 million appeared first on Protos.
item.content:encoded:
CoreWeave CEO Mike Intrator sold about $85 million worth of stock in the heavily indebted AI company between September 15 and September 30.

Those same shares have since lost more than a quarter of their value.

Insider selling is rampant at the company whose stock has lost $18 billion in market cap and more than 46% of its share price since joining the Nasdaq 100 index.

  • CFO Nitin Agrawal sold at about $80 a share on Monday. 
  • CRO Jonathan Jones sold at about $77 on Tuesday, while the company’s cost to borrow skyrocketed to 15% annually on its 2032 bonds and shares plunged 15% one day later.
  • General counsel Kristen McVeety sold 97,500 shares near $94 on September 8, taking in $9 million. 
  • Co-founder Brannin McBee sold 250,000 shares at about $106 on August 17, raising $27 million for himself.

This week, McBee told the Financial Times that CoreWeave is looking to borrow even more money.

Read more: CoreWeave down 32% since joining the Nasdaq 100

CEO sells cheaper and cheaper CoreWeave stock

Although the CEO has sold a regular, weekly block of about 307,700 shares, the value of his sales has been collapsing alongside CoreWeave’s stock price. 

  • On May 5, that block fetched $39 million at about $128 per share.
  • On September 8, it raised $31 million near $100 per share.
  • On September 22, it yielded $27 million near $87 per share. 
  • At Thursday’s price near $60, his block would bring in less than $19 million.

All told, officers and directors have sold about $740 million of CoreWeave stock since the company joined the normally prestigious Nasdaq 100 index on June 22.

Shares opened that day near $119 yet opened for trading today below $62. Lenders to the company are pricing distress.

CoreWeave’s cost to borrow on 2031 maturity bonds soared above 16% — nearing credit card interest rates. 

Credit default swaps on CoreWeave implied roughly a 63% chance of default within five years.

At the end of June, the company owed roughly $52 billion in combined debt and lease obligations.

item.title: Tether paid Bo Hines’ company while he was at White House, WSJ
item.dc:creator: REDACTED
item.description:
Tether reportedly paid Nxum, a firm founded by Bo Hines, millions of dollars while he was in his role at the White House.

The post Tether paid Bo Hines’ company while he was at White House, WSJ appeared first on Protos.
item.content:encoded:
Before Bo Hines became chief executive officer of Tether-backed stablecoin USAT, he was President Donald Trump’s executive director of the President’s Council of Advisers on Digital Assets.

While he was serving the president and working to advance stablecoin legislation, Tether — the world’s largest stablecoin — was reportedly partnering with Nxum Capital, an investment and consulting firm that Hines started with his father.

According to reporting from The Wall Street Journal (WSJ), “Nxum has earned $6.3 million” from the deal to help create a “strategic brand and public affairs plan” for Tether.

This money was apparently sent via Tether sister fund, Bitfinex, to Notorious, a firm led by Peter Vincer, who then forwarded the lion’s share of the funds to Nxum.

The report claims that Tether sent its first $2.49 million payment from Bitfinex to Vincer on May 11, 2025. Vincer kept $498,000 and sent the rest to a Nxum wallet, where it was split three ways.

On May 11, 2025, 0x77134cbC06cB00b66F4c7e623D5fdBF6777635EC, an address labeled as “Bitfinex: Hot Wallet” on Etherscan, sent $2.49 million in USDT to 0x4b3e4956a5Bf253Cf28f8cf9b9F71BfD100E98Fd across two transactions, with the $1 test transaction actually occurring the day before.

Following this, all but $498,000 was transferred to 0xA6078664175FCfb093989EC778C03FAe58170814.

The funds were then, according to WSJ, split three ways. We cannot be absolutely certain these are the same transactions, but they do match the details we know so far.

Vincer apparently told WSJ that he was the intermediary for the deal, and after Hines left the White House, the contract was transferred directly to Nxum.

A Nxum representative told WSJ that Hines “did not receive any Tether-derived funds during that period, and had no economic relationship of any kind with Tether while serving in the White House.”

While in the White House, Hines was apparently still exchanging Signal messages with his company partners. He shared details about the Genius Act with Nxum leaders who were working with Tether.

Read more: Tether took over the White House, now it’s tearing it down to build a ballroom

Nxum has been involved in politics as well, supporting the Fellowship PAC.

This super PAC is chaired by Jesse Spiro, Tether’s head of government affairs. It’s raised $11 million dollars, with $10 million coming from Tether custodian Cantor Fitzgerald, the firm previously led by Commerce Secretary, Howard Lutnick.

The remaining funds came from Anchor Labs, Inc., a firm associated with Anchorage Digital, the bank behind USAT.

This super PAC has paid out $11 million to Nxum, though there was also a $300,000 refund.

The GENIUS Act was eventually signed into law in July 2025, with Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino appearing at the White House to signal his support. The next month Hines announced he was leaving the White House.

The month after that, it was announced that Hines would be leading USAT, with Tether referencing his entrepreneurial history as a motivator.

Protos reached out to Tether for comment (and attempted to reach out to Nxum, but its previous contact email is now undeliverable), but it did not immediately respond.

item.title: FBI helps smash crypto scam targeting Russian speakers in Brooklyn
item.dc:creator: REDACTED
item.description:
The FBI worked with Brooklyn's Virtual Currency Unit to take down hundreds of servers and domains that aided the crypto scam network.

The post FBI helps smash crypto scam targeting Russian speakers in Brooklyn appeared first on Protos.
item.content:encoded:
The FBI has helped take down a crypto scam network that targeted Russian-speaking individuals living in the US and likely stole tens of millions of dollars. 

The operation, described as “one of the biggest operational cyber disruptions undertaken by a local prosecutor’s office,” was led by Brooklyn District Attorney Eric Gonzalez’s Virtual Currency Unit (VCU). 

Russian-speaking people living in Brooklyn were targeted by crypto scammers operating a phony forex investment site that promised substantial returns via Russian-tailored ads. 

Read more: Elliptic chief: Tether and Telegram prop up $442B scam economy

Individuals were contacted by fake investment advisors and convinced into depositing funds on their supposed investment site.

Victims were shown fake gains, and when they tried to withdraw their funds, they were told their account was locked or that they had to pay more money to access it. 

Crypto scammers hit victims with more recovery scams

Authorities dismantled 241 crypto scam domains and 112 servers across Ukraine, Eastern Europe, and America.  

The group would also revisit individuals it had already scammed, luring them with recovery operations that promised to restore their stolen crypto. 

Gonzalez’s local office was able to seize $300,000, but despite this, many Individuals lost their life savings. 

FBI director’s Russia optics aren’t great right now

FBI Director Kash Patel is also making headlines in relation to Russia. 

MS NOW reported that Patel had landed in Russia on Wednesday for a two-day meeting with the country’s Federal Security Service (FSB). 

However, US authorities clarified that he was in fact attending a law enforcement event in Virginia on that day. 

Patel then posted on X, “From Russia, with love…” after the event.

Read more: Crypto hacking group ShinyHunters says it stole data of 5,000 FBI agents

This received considerable backlash, with X users highlighting the different ways the US is currently helping Russia. 

Russia and the US recently signed a deal that would see Ukraine’s attacker trade 300,000 barrels of diesel with the US. The US is also slated to get a further 500,000 in November, and a million “immediately thereafter.”

item.title: GTA 6 leaker threatens dead man’s switch for endgame spoilers
item.dc:creator: REDACTED
item.description:
Pseudonymous GTA 6 leaker “Cyberleek” has threatened to reveal the long-awaited game’s ending if they're caught.

The post GTA 6 leaker threatens dead man’s switch for endgame spoilers appeared first on Protos.
item.content:encoded:
Pseudonymous GTA 6 leaker “Cyberleek” has threatened to reveal the long-awaited game’s ending if they’re caught, but won’t be leaking content regularly anymore because of their poorly performing crypto token.  

Last week, Protos reported that Cyberleek had ended their hiatus to drop more GTA 6 leaks with an emphasis on nudity. 

It pumped their cryptocurrency by 200% over two days, which, despite the positive price action, wasn’t as good as the $40 million market cap it achieved when the first leaks were revealed. 

However, Cyberleek is now struggling again. According to their latest message this morning, they claim that they won’t leak the game’s full build as their token was unable to reach a market cap of $30 million.

Read more: GTA VI leaker’s token crashes despite ‘first true spoiler’

Right now, the token’s market cap sits at a little over $1 million. It reportedly began to crash after they announced a roadmap of several million-dollar market cap leak milestones. 

Cyberleek still threatens GTA 6 endgame spoilers

Despite this, Cyberleek still claims they can leak the game’s ending, and as evidence, claimed to show out-of-context clips of the final story missions. 

Rather than leak it outright, they’ve threatened a “dead man’s switch” that will spoil the game’s ending if they’re ever caught. 

They claim it would ruin the experience for gamers and that Rockstar Games’ parent company, Take-Two, “was punished enough.”

Read more: GTA VI leak investigation video raises crypto scam suspicions

GTA 6 is currently set to release on November 19. 

People Make Games co-founder Chris Bratt claims that an employment tribunal between Rockstar Games and 34 fired workers was delayed by a month to November 17 and 18. 

Bratt says this is because Rockstar Games asked for more time for its lawyers to cross-examine certain employees. 

X users have since begun to speculate that the specific employees may in fact be Cyberleek.

item.title: Strategy’s USD Cash down 60% in seven weeks
item.dc:creator: REDACTED
item.description:
Strategy’s USD Cash pile has plummeted 60% from $1.61B in late August to just $640.5M a few days ago.

The post Strategy’s USD Cash down 60% in seven weeks appeared first on Protos.
item.content:encoded:
USD Cash at Michael Saylor’s BTC treasury company Strategy has fallen 60% from $1.61 billion on August 30 to $640.5 million on October 11, according to its latest disclosure this week.

The firm has spent the majority of its USD Cash on STRC buybacks, Strategy’s ultra-high yield dividend stock that it sold to investors for $90–100.03 per share before those same shares briefly collapsed to $71.25.

Reinstilling confidence that the shares would trade near their intended $100 price has cost the company — especially common shareholders — extensive cash that the company mostly raised via common shareholder dilution.

Read more: Strategy’s USD reserve didn’t last long

Strategy’s pace of USD Cash depletion works out to about $970 million in less than seven weeks. If it continues that average pace and doesn’t top it up, its USD Cash will run out in about four weeks.

Amid the aforementioned buybacks, Saylor has taken to X to post glowing reviews about STRC’s recovery. This included another installment of his imaginary retiree supposedly enjoying a carefree lifestyle funded by STRC dividends.

Pretend to not check the price of STRC

The unbothered, AI-generated investor doesn’t even bother to check the price of STRC.

Although irresponsible, choosing to bury one’s head in the sand certainly would have saved any real investor the gut-punch of STRC’s actual price whipsawing 29% since Saylor first broadcasted her testimonial from his social media feed on March 30.

Read more: Strategy has burned through 64% of its STRC rescue fund

Strategy’s August USD Cash figure included expected proceeds from stock sales that hadn’t yet settled, but the starting figure is accurate by Strategy’s own accounting with that footnote.

Moreover, USD Cash isn’t Strategy’s only dollar stockpile, due to a separate “USD Reserve,” earmarked for bond coupons and dividend payments, holding $4.88 billion as of October 11.

That reserve is down from the $5.10 billion it reported for August 30.

The combined change of both USD reserves is still decidedly negative, albeit slightly less dramatically at approximately 18% combined.

Strategy’s two piles of USD cash

Strategy created USD Cash on August 24, funding most of it with about $1.57 billion from the sale of roughly $2 billion of MSTR stock the week prior.

Common shareholders, as usual, paid for Strategy executives’ flexibility by suffering dilution of their MSTR shares.

The company explained at the time, “USD Cash complements the USD Reserve by providing management with a more flexible source of liquidity for the purposes described above.”

In plain English, executives gave themselves a second pot of cash from which they could spend more freely.

The older USD Reserve had stricter limits. Strategy may use this reserve for preferred dividends and interest payments, unless its board formally authorizes otherwise.

It paid out $142.5 million for those purposes during the week of October 4, for example.

Strategy’s board doubled its STRC total buyback authorization to $2 billion in September, yet just $354.8 million of that authorized amount remained as of October 11.

item.title: Bank of America hit with $1.2B fine after missing ‘Chinese money laundering’
item.dc:creator: REDACTED
item.description:
Bank of America processed over $5B in suspicious transactions, including "transactions indicative of Chinese Money Laundering Networks."

The post Bank of America hit with $1.2B fine after missing ‘Chinese money laundering’ appeared first on Protos.
item.content:encoded:
Bank of America has been fined a total of $1.2 billion dollars by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) after admitting failures of its Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and anti-money laundering (AML) compliance program resulting in over $5 billion in suspicious activity.

The $750 million fine from the OCC is the largest civil money penalty that the bureau has ever issued.

FinCEN is responsible for the remainder of the fine and credits the $750 million against its total penalty of $1.2 billion.

Read more: How a money launderer allegedly used Deltec, Binance, and Tether

The FinCEN order details how Bank of America “willfully failed to implement and maintain adequate internal controls for BSA compliance” which resulted in missing or delayed reports for “over $5 billion of suspicious activity, with roughly $1 billion of this activity implicating national security-related and other priority illicit finance risks, including suspicious transactions indicative of Chinese Money Laundering Networks.”

This Chinese Money Laundering Network activity included “high volumes of back-to-back credit card purchases at major retailers and shipping companies inconsistent with customer profiles,” and “regular, large-value ACH and bill pay transactions to pay off balances for credit cards issued by third-party financial institutions.

These included “cards in the name of third-party individuals for which there was no apparent commercial purpose; large wire transfers to counterparties in China with generic descriptions (e.g., “for goods”) and no discernible business rationale; and substantial, repeated transfers to counterparties with no web presence operating from residential addresses, demonstrating an apparent lack of legitimate commercial purpose.”

Additionally, FinCEN found that the bank’s due diligence on correspondent accounts held by its own foreign branches and affiliates fell short.

Some regulatory questionnaires “were completed by the bank on behalf of all its foreign branches and affiliates, and others were completed for specific foreign branches and affiliates.”

This record-breaking OCC fine follows its recent $350 million fine levied against American Express.

item.title: OpenAI eyes security firm purchase amid office bugging scandal
item.dc:creator: REDACTED
item.description:
The AI giant behind ChatGPT is reportedly in talks with Trail of Bits, a security auditor which counts many top crypto projects as clients.

The post OpenAI eyes security firm purchase amid office bugging scandal appeared first on Protos.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI is in talks to acquire Trail of Bits (ToB), a cybersecurity firm which counts top crypto projects among its clients, according to a Tuesday report by The Information.

The news comes in the wake of a major security incident at the AI giant’s offices, in which it discovered a “sophisticated recording device” in a conference room, planted by an engineer who’s since been arrested by the FBI.

ToB is one of the best known and well-respected auditors among crypto projects, with experience in nine blockchain ecosystems, and counting Arbitrum, Uniswap and Aave as clients.

Read more: Ledger spyware scare spreads beyond Southeast Asia

OpenAI and ToB previously collaborated on the “Patch the Planet” initiative, part of OpenAI’s wider Daybreak frontier model security program. In 2023, it also audited World (then Worldcoin), with which OpenAI shares a co-founder, Sam Altman.

Earlier this year, ToB produced a set of plug-ins for “security research, vulnerability detection, and audit workflows” via Claude Code, including smart contract vulnerability scanning.

Red teaming

The potential acquisition comes after a major reckoning for top AI companies and the dangers they present.

The discussion kicked off after a rogue swarm of OpenAI agents broke out of their sandbox and attacked the open-source AI platform HuggingFace in July.

While the increasing need for security expertise is clear, both within crypto and the wider AI industry, some find the potential for gatekeeping worrying.

Read more: Claude AI plugins can now vibe code smart contracts

Conversely, Yuga Labs’ 0xQuit called the move “extremely bullish” for crypto security, while another X user suspects OpenAI may be making a move into agentic crypto adoption.

A ToB audit is far from a rubber-stamp for safety, however.

DeFi projects audited by the firm have been exploited in the past, including Balancer and Bunni Finance, which lost $129 million and $8 million, respectively, last year.

Balancer has since decided to shut down.

item.title: Richard Heart arrested in Turkey almost 2 years after Interpol red notice
item.dc:creator: REDACTED
item.description:
Hex founder Richard Heart was reportedly arrested in Istanbul in a raid that saw three handguns, four rifles, and millions in cash seized.

The post Richard Heart arrested in Turkey almost 2 years after Interpol red notice appeared first on Protos.
item.content:encoded:
Richard Heart, the Hex founder wanted by Finland under an Interpol Red Notice, was reportedly arrested by police in Istanbul on Wednesday. 

That’s according to Turkish news outlet Haberler, which reports that during the morning raid, police seized $4 million in cash, 64 luxury watches, guns, computers, crypto mining equipment, and other electronic devices from Heart, real name Richard James Schueler. 

Euronews reports that three handguns, four rifles, seven magazines, 1,360 rounds of ammunition, and a dagger were also seized. 

Read more: Finland wants to detain Richard Heart, alleges millions in unpaid taxes

Istanbul’s National Intelligence Organization (MİT) and local Beşiktaş police conducted the raid, which was coordinated by Istanbul’s Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office, Financial Crimes Divison, Interpol, and MİT. 

Haberler reports that the investigation looked into Schueler’s alleged Istanbul-based international fraud network that also held offices across the US, Finland, and Spain.

The price of Schueler’s Hex token plunged almost 45% following the news of his arrest.

US doesn’t want Richard Heart arrested — but Finland does

In 2023, the SEC accused Heart of selling over $1 billion in unregistered securities, and misappropriating millions of dollars from his Hex, PulseChain, and PulseX crypto projects.

He allegedly misused $12 million to purchase sports cars, watches, and a 555-carat black diamond known as “The Enigma.”

Two years later, the lawsuit was dropped after the SEC failed to establish legal jurisdiction. He’s also no longer listed on Europol’s most wanted list, likely due to today’s reported arrest.

Read more: Richard Heart tells court full of US investors that HEX wasn’t aimed at them

An Interpol Red Notice on behalf of Finland was posted in December 2024 for alleged aggravated tax fraud involving hundreds of millions of euros in unpaid tax. 

He also allegedly assaulted a minor in 2021.

Heart’s alleged new abode in Istanbul was a luxurious address, potentially paid for using funds linked to suspected crypto mixer transactions through which Heart attempted to obfuscate $500 million worth of crypto.
